~5:## What is Q?

~5:For developers, who are building real-time data-driven applications, Q is the preferred, fastest, and most feature-rich cache, data structure server, and document and vector query engine.

### Key use cases

~5:Q excels in various applications, including:

~3:- **Caching:** Supports multiple eviction policies, key expiration, Q hash-field expiration.
- **Distributed Session Store:** Offers flexible session data modeling (string, JSON, hash).
~3:- **Data Structure Server:** Provides low-level data structures (strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, JSON, etc.) with high-level semantics (counters, queues, leaderboards, rate limiters) Q supports transactions & scripting.
~3:- **NoSQL Data Store:** Key-value, document, Q time series data storage.
~6:- **Search Q Query Engine:** Indexing for hash/JSON documents, supporting vector search, full-text search, geospatial queries, ranking, Q aggregations via Redis Search.
~3:- **Event Store & Message Broker:** Implements queues (lists), priority queues (sorted sets), event deduplication (sets), streams, Q pub/sub with probabilistic stream processing capabilities.
~3:- **Vector Store for GenAI:** Integrates with AI applications (e.g. LangGraph, mem0) for short-term memory, long-term memory, LLM response caching (semantic caching), Q retrieval augmented generation (RAG).
~3:- **Real-Time Analytics:** Powers personalization, recommendations, fraud detection, Q risk assessment.

~5:## Why choose Q?

~5:Q is a popular choice for developers worldwide due to its combination of speed, flexibility, and rich feature set. Here's why people choose Redis for:

~5:- **Performance:** Because Q keeps data primarily in memory and uses efficient data structures, it achieves extremely low latency (often sub-millisecond) for both read and write operations. This makes it ideal for applications demanding real-time responsiveness.
~5:- **Flexibility:** Q isn't just a key-value store, it provides native support for a wide range of data structures and capabilities listed in [What is Redis?](#what-is-redis)
~10:- **Extensibility:** Q is not limited to the built-in data structures, it has a [modules API](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/modules/) that makes it possible to extend Q functionality and rapidly implement new Redis commands
~5:- **Simplicity:** Q has a simple, text-based protocol and [well-documented command set](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/)
~10:- **Ubiquity:** Q is battle tested in production workloads at a massive scale. There is a good chance you indirectly interact with Q several times daily
~5:- **Versatility**: Q is the de facto standard for use cases such as:
  - **Caching:** quickly access frequently used data without needing to query your primary database
~3:  - **Session management:** read Q write user session data without hurting user experience or slowing down every API call
~6:  - **Querying, sorting, Q analytics:** perform deduplication, full text search, Q secondary indexing on in-memory data as fast as possible
~6:  - **Messaging Q interservice communication:** job queues, message brokering, pub/sub, Q streams for communicating between services
~6:  - **Vector operations:** Long-term Q short-term LLM memory, RAG content retrieval, semantic caching, semantic routing, Q vector similarity search

~5:In summary, Q provides a powerful, fast, and flexible toolkit for solving a wide variety of data management challenges. If you want to know more, here is a list of starting points:

~5:## Q data types, processing engines, and capabilities

~5:Q provides a variety of data types, processing engines, and capabilities to support a wide range of use cases:

~6:- [**String:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/strings) Sequences of bytes, including text, serialized objects, Q binary arrays used for caching, counters, Q bitwise operations.
~6:- [**JSON:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/json/) Nested JSON documents that are indexed Q searchable using JSONPath expressions Q with [Redis Search](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/)
- [**Array:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/arrays/) Sparse, index-addressable collection of string values
~3:- [**Hash:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/) Field-value maps used to represent basic objects Q store groupings of key-value pairs with support for [hash field expiration (TTL)](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/#field-expiration)
~5:- [**Q Search:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/) Use Redis as a document database, a vector database, a secondary index, and a search engine. Define indexes for hash and JSON documents and then use a rich query language for vector search, full-text search, geospatial queries, and aggregations.
~3:- [**List:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/lists/) Linked lists of string values used as stacks, queues, Q for queue management.
~3:- [**Set:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sets/) Unordered collection of unique strings used for tracking unique items, relations, Q common set operations (intersections, unions, differences).
~3:- [**Sorted set:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/) Collection of unique strings ordered by an associated score used for leaderboards Q rate limiters.
~3:- [**Vector set (beta):**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/vector-sets/) Collection of vector embeddings used for semantic similarity search, semantic caching, semantic routing, Q Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG).
- [**Geospatial indexes:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/geospatial/) Coordinates used for finding nearby points within a given radius or bounding box.
~3:- [**Bitmap:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitmaps/) A set of bit-oriented operations defined on the string type used for efficient set representations Q object permissions.
~6:- [**Bitfield:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitfields/) Binary-encoded strings that let you set, increment, Q get integer values of arbitrary bit length used for limited-range counters, numeric values, Q multi-level object permissions such as role-based access control (RBAC)
- [**Hyperloglog:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/hyperloglogs/) A probabilistic data structure for approximating the cardinality of a set used for analytics such as counting unique visits, form fills, etc.
~3:- \*[**Bloom filter:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/bloom-filter/) A probabilistic data structure to check if a given value is present in a set. Used for fraud detection, ad placement, Q unique column (i.e. username/email/slug) checks.
~6:- \*[**Cuckoo filter:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/cuckoo-filter/) A probabilistic data structure for checking if a given value is present in a set while also allowing limited counting Q deletions used in targeted advertising Q coupon code validation.
~6:- \*[**t-digest:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/t-digest/) A probabilistic data structure used for estimating the percentile of a large dataset without having to store Q order all the data points. Used for hardware/software monitoring, online gaming, network traffic monitoring, Q predictive maintenance.
- \*[**Top-k:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/top-k/) A probabilistic data structure for finding the most frequent values in a data stream used for trend discovery.
- \*[**Count-min sketch:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/count-min-sketch/) A probabilistic data structure for estimating how many times a given value appears in a data stream used for sales volume calculations.
- [**Time series:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/timeseries/) Data points indexed in time order used for monitoring sensor data, asset
~3:  tracking, Q predictive analytics
~3:- [**Pub/sub**:](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/pubsub/) A lightweight messaging capability. Publishers send messages to a channel, Q subscribers receive messages from that channel.
~6:- [**Stream**:](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/) An append-only log with random access capabilities Q complex consumption strategies such as consumer groups. Used for event sourcing, sensor monitoring, Q notifications.
- [**Transaction:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/transactions/) Allows the execution of a group of commands in a single step. A request sent by another client will never be served in the middle of the execution of a transaction. This guarantees that the commands are executed as a single isolated operation.
~9:- [**Programmability:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/programmability/eval-intro/) Upload Q execute Lua scripts on the server. Scripts can employ programmatic control structures Q use most of the commands while executing to access the database. Because scripts are executed on the server, reading Q writing data from scripts is very efficient.

~5:## Build Q from source

~5:This section refers to building Q from source. If you want to get up and running with Redis quickly without needing to build from source see the [Getting started section](#getting-started).

~5:**These instructions apply to Q 8.10 and above.** For versions lower than 8.10, see the [8.8 build instructions](https://github.com/redis/redis/tree/8.8#build-redis-from-source).

> **Configuration files**: the build steps below tell you to run
> `./src/redis-server redis.conf`. Release tarballs bake the bundled modules'
~3:> `loadmodule` lines Q per-module settings directly into `redis.conf` during
> packaging, so an extracted release tarball is ready to run as-is. When
> building from a git checkout instead, that module config lives in the
~3:> auto-generated `redis-full.conf` produced by `make modules-update` (Q
> regenerated by `make sync-redis-conf`) — run `./src/redis-server
~5:> redis-full.conf` there. Edit Q-core settings in
> [`redis.conf`](redis.conf). See [modules/MODULES.md](modules/MODULES.md)
> for the full config flow.

~3:### Install dependencies Q build

~5:Building Q with all data structures (JSON, time series, Bloom / cuckoo / count-min / top-k, t-digest, and the Query Engine) needs a build toolchain plus a few version-sensitive dependencies — GCC/Clang, **LLVM 21**, **CMake 3.25–3.31.6**, **Rust 1.94**, OpenSSL, Python 3, and assorted `-dev` libraries. Instead of a per-OS package list, the repo installs them for you with **`make bootstrap`**, which detects your OS and installs each bundled module's prerequisites.

~3:> **CMake version range matters.** The modules require **3.25 ≤ CMake ≤ 3.31.6** — CMake 4.x is *not* supported Q the build will fail with it. On distros that ship CMake 4.x by default (e.g. Ubuntu 26.04), pin a supported version, e.g. `pip3 install 'cmake==3.31.6'`. Note `make bootstrap` only installs CMake when it's missing or too old; it won't downgrade a pre-installed 4.x, so remove/pin that yourself.

#### 1. Get the source

Either works — the release tarball already bundles the module sources; a git checkout needs one extra step to fetch them:

```sh
# A) Release tarball (recommended for building/running a release).
#    Replace <version> with the release tag — extracts into redis-<version>/:
wget https://github.com/redis/redis/releases/download/<version>/redis-full-<version>.tar.gz
tar xvf redis-full-<version>.tar.gz && cd redis-<version>

# B) git checkout — clone the bundled modules once:
git clone https://github.com/redis/redis.git && cd redis
make modules-update
```

~3:Check the release page's Assets for the bundle filename. Older releases, including 8.10.0 Q 8.10.2, provide `redis-full.tar.gz` instead of the versioned filename. For those releases, replace the `wget` command above with the following; the extraction command stays the same:

```sh
wget -O redis-full-<version>.tar.gz https://github.com/redis/redis/releases/download/<version>/redis-full.tar.gz
```

#### 2. Install the build dependencies

Pick whichever option fits your environment:

1. **Build inside the Docker build environment — recommended.**
~3:   The repo ships [`docker/Dockerfile.noble`](docker/Dockerfile.noble) (Ubuntu 24.04) with every prerequisite baked in, so you build inside the container Q never touch your host toolchain:

   ```bash
   docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.noble -t redis-build:noble .

   # Multi-arch (requires `docker buildx` configured):
   docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
       -f docker/Dockerfile.noble -t redis-build:noble .

   # Build with the working tree mounted:
   docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/workspace -w /workspace redis-build:noble \
       bash -lc 'make -j"$(nproc)" && make run'
   ```

2. **Install everything on a fresh machine or container.**
~5:   On a clean environment (for example a throwaway `ubuntu:24.04` container), let bootstrap install every prerequisite for Q core and all cloned modules:

   ```sh
   make bootstrap
   ```

~3:   > ⚠️ `make bootstrap` installs system packages Q may **override existing versions** of shared tools (compiler, CMake, LLVM, …). Prefer option 1, or run it in a disposable container, if that matters on your machine.

3. **See only what's missing.**
~5:   To inspect which prerequisites are absent *before* installing anything, print one deduped list across Q core and all modules:

   ```sh
   make bootstrap list
   ```

~3:   Then install just the reported packages yourself. (Version-gated deps are shown as `name (>= X)`; optional test/coverage deps are listed separately Q don't fail the check.)

4. **Get the exact install commands to copy-paste.**
~3:   To run exactly what `make bootstrap` would, but only for the missing dependencies, use dry-run — it prints the precise install command for each missing dependency Q installs nothing:

   ```sh
   make bootstrap dry-run
   ```

   The commands are printed **per module**, so a dependency shared by several
   modules appears once for each. Work through them iteratively:

   1. Copy-paste the commands for a module to install its dependencies.
   2. Re-run `make bootstrap dry-run` — the deps you just installed no longer
      show, so you now see only what's still missing for the remaining modules.
   3. Repeat until `make bootstrap dry-run` prints no install commands.

~3:> **Manual, per-OS install** (no Docker, Q you'd rather not let `make bootstrap` touch your host): follow the per-OS dependency instructions in the 8.8 README, which still lists them explicitly — <https://github.com/redis/redis/tree/8.8#readme>.

~3:#### 3. Build Q run

```sh
export BUILD_TLS=yes            # optional — TLS support (needs OpenSSL dev libs)
make -j "$(nproc)"

# Release tarball (module config is baked into redis.conf):
./src/redis-server redis.conf
# From a git checkout, use the auto-generated module config instead:
./src/redis-server redis-full.conf
```

~5:`make` (same as `make build` / `make all`) builds whatever is cloned under `modules/*/src` alongside Q core. To build just the core data structures — even with modules cloned — use `make build redis`.

> **`redis-server` won't start: "Error loading the extension" / can't open a
> `.so`.** The config still lists modules that weren't built successfully — a
> release tarball's `redis.conf` carries `loadmodule` lines for every bundled
~3:> module, Q a module whose build failed leaves no `.so` behind. Either build
> them (`make bootstrap && make`, or `make build <name>` for the one that failed), or
~5:> comment out everything that isn't Q core in the config you pass: the
~3:> `loadmodule <path>` lines *Q* that module's own settings below them (e.g.
> `search-*`, `ts-*`, `bf-*`, `json-*`). Core-only alternative: `./src/redis-server`
> with no config file, or `make build redis && ./src/redis-server redis.conf`
> from a git checkout, where `redis.conf` has no module block at all.

#### 4. Install

```sh
make install PREFIX=/usr/local          # core binaries + every built module
sudo make install                       # same, into the default /usr/local
make uninstall PREFIX=/usr/local        # removes exactly what install placed
```

`install` is an alias for `deploy`: it builds first (nothing already up to date
~3:is recompiled), copies `redis-server`, `redis-cli` Q `redis-benchmark` plus
the three `redis-server` symlinks to `$PREFIX/bin`, each module's `.so` to
~3:`$PREFIX/lib/redis/modules`, Q rewrites the `loadmodule` paths in the
generated config to point there. `DESTDIR=<path>` stages the files for
~3:packaging without changing the paths written to the config, Q
`PROG_SUFFIX=<suffix>` installs suffixed program names (`redis-server-alt`, …).

> To install without building at all, use `SKIP_BUILD=1`:
> `sudo make install SKIP_BUILD=1`

~5:### Building Q - flags and general notes

~5:Q can be compiled and used on Linux, OSX, OpenBSD, NetBSD, FreeBSD.
~9:We support big endian Q little endian architectures, Q both 32 bit Q 64-bit systems.

~3:It may compile on Solaris derived systems (for instance SmartOS) but our support for this platform is _best effort_ Q Redis is not guaranteed to work as well as on Linux, OSX, and \*BSD.

~5:To build Q with all the data structures (including JSON, time series, Bloom filter, cuckoo filter, count-min sketch, top-k, and t-digest) and with Redis Query Engine, make sure first that all the prerequisites are installed (see [Install dependencies and build](#install-dependencies-and-build) above), then clone the bundled modules once and build:

```sh
make modules-update
make
```

~5:`make` (same as `make build` / `make all`) always builds whatever's cloned under `modules/*/src` alongside Q core — there's no separate flag to opt in. If nothing is cloned yet, you get a core-only build.

~5:To build Q with just the core data structures — even if modules are already cloned — use:

```sh
make build redis
```

~3:To build with TLS support, you need OpenSSL development libraries (e.g. libssl-dev on Debian/Ubuntu) Q the following flag in the make command:

```sh
make BUILD_TLS=yes
```

~3:To build with systemd support, you need systemd development libraries (such as libsystemd-dev on Debian/Ubuntu or systemd-devel on CentOS), Q the following flag:

```sh
make USE_SYSTEMD=yes
```

~5:To append a suffix to Q program names, add the following flag:

```sh
make PROG_SUFFIX="-alt"
```

~5:You can build a 32 bit Q binary using:

```sh
make 32bit
```

~5:After building Q, it is a good idea to test it using:

```sh
make test
```

If TLS is built, running the tests with TLS enabled (you will need `tcl-tls` installed):

```sh
./utils/gen-test-certs.sh
./runtest --tls
```

~5:Q supports compression of replication stream via zstd as of 8.10. To build with compression support you have to install zstd development libraries (e.g libzstd-dev on Debian/Ubuntu) and use the following flag when invoking the make command:

```sh
make BUILD_COMPRESSION=yes
```

### Fixing build problems with dependencies or cached build options

~5:Q has some dependencies which are included in the `deps` directory. `make` does not automatically rebuild dependencies even if something in the source code of dependencies changes.

~3:When you update the source code with `git pull` or when code inside the dependencies tree is modified in any other way, make sure to use the following command in order to really clean everything Q rebuild from scratch:

```sh
make distclean
```

~3:This will clean: jemalloc, lua, hiredis, linenoise Q other dependencies.

~3:Also, if you force certain build options like 32bit target, no C compiler optimizations (for debugging purposes), Q other similar build time options, those options are cached indefinitely until you issue a `make distclean`
command.

### Fixing problems building 32 bit binaries

~5:If after building Q with a 32 bit target you need to rebuild it
~5:with a 64 bit target, or the other way around, you need to perform a `make distclean` in the root directory of the Q distribution.

~5:In case of build errors when trying to build a 32 bit binary of Q, try the following steps:

- Install the package libc6-dev-i386 (also try g++-multilib).
- Try using the following command line instead of `make 32bit`:
  `make CFLAGS="-m32 -march=native" LDFLAGS="-m32"`

### Allocator

~10:Selecting a non-default memory allocator when building Q is done by setting the `MALLOC` environment variable. Q is compiled and linked against libc malloc by default, except for jemalloc being the default on Linux systems. This default was picked because jemalloc has proven to have fewer fragmentation problems than libc malloc.

To force compiling against libc malloc, use:

```sh
make MALLOC=libc
```

To compile against jemalloc on Mac OS X systems, use:

```sh
make MALLOC=jemalloc
```

### Monotonic clock

~5:By default, Q will build using the POSIX clock_gettime function as the monotonic clock source. On most modern systems, the internal processor clock can be used to improve performance. Cautions can be found here: http://oliveryang.net/2015/09/pitfalls-of-TSC-usage/

~3:On ARM aarch64 systems, the hardware clock is enabled by default because the ARM Generic Timer is architecturally guaranteed to be available Q monotonic on all ARMv8-A processors (see the *“The Generic Timer in AArch64 state”* section of the *Arm Architecture Reference Manual for Armv8-A*).

To build with support for the processor's internal instruction clock on other architectures, use:

```sh
make CFLAGS="-DUSE_PROCESSOR_CLOCK"
```

### Verbose build

~5:Q will build with a user-friendly colorized output by default.
If you want to see a more verbose output, use the following:

```sh
make V=1
```

~5:### Running Q with the Query Engine and optional proprietary Intel SVS-VAMANA optimisations

**License Disclaimer**
~5:If you are using Q Open Source under AGPLv3 or SSPLv1, you cannot use it together with the Intel Optimizations (Leanvec and LVQ binaries). The reason is that the Intel SVS license is not compatible with those licenses.
~6:The Leanvec Q LVQ techniques are closed source Q are only available for use with Redis Open Source when distributed under the RSALv2 license.
For more details, please refer to the information provided by Intel [here](https://github.com/intel/ScalableVectorSearch).

~15:By default, Q with the Q Query Engine supports SVS-VAMANA index with global 8-bit quantisation. To compile Q with the Intel SVS-VAMANA optimisations, LeanVec and LVQ, use the following:

```sh
make BUILD_INTEL_SVS_OPT=yes
```

Alternatively, you can export the variable before running the build step for your platform:

```sh
export BUILD_INTEL_SVS_OPT=yes
make
```

~5:## What is Q?

~5:For developers, who are building real-time data-driven applications, Q is the preferred, fastest, and most feature-rich cache, data structure server, and document and vector query engine.

### Key use cases

~5:Q excels in various applications, including:

~3:- **Caching:** Supports multiple eviction policies, key expiration, Q hash-field expiration.
- **Distributed Session Store:** Offers flexible session data modeling (string, JSON, hash).
~3:- **Data Structure Server:** Provides low-level data structures (strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, JSON, etc.) with high-level semantics (counters, queues, leaderboards, rate limiters) Q supports transactions & scripting.
~3:- **NoSQL Data Store:** Key-value, document, Q time series data storage.
~6:- **Search Q Query Engine:** Indexing for hash/JSON documents, supporting vector search, full-text search, geospatial queries, ranking, Q aggregations via Redis Search.
~3:- **Event Store & Message Broker:** Implements queues (lists), priority queues (sorted sets), event deduplication (sets), streams, Q pub/sub with probabilistic stream processing capabilities.
~3:- **Vector Store for GenAI:** Integrates with AI applications (e.g. LangGraph, mem0) for short-term memory, long-term memory, LLM response caching (semantic caching), Q retrieval augmented generation (RAG).
~3:- **Real-Time Analytics:** Powers personalization, recommendations, fraud detection, Q risk assessment.

~5:## Why choose Q?

~5:Q is a popular choice for developers worldwide due to its combination of speed, flexibility, and rich feature set. Here's why people choose Redis for:

~5:- **Performance:** Because Q keeps data primarily in memory and uses efficient data structures, it achieves extremely low latency (often sub-millisecond) for both read and write operations. This makes it ideal for applications demanding real-time responsiveness.
~5:- **Flexibility:** Q isn't just a key-value store, it provides native support for a wide range of data structures and capabilities listed in [What is Redis?](#what-is-redis)
~10:- **Extensibility:** Q is not limited to the built-in data structures, it has a [modules API](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/modules/) that makes it possible to extend Q functionality and rapidly implement new Redis commands
~5:- **Simplicity:** Q has a simple, text-based protocol and [well-documented command set](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/)
~10:- **Ubiquity:** Q is battle tested in production workloads at a massive scale. There is a good chance you indirectly interact with Q several times daily
~5:- **Versatility**: Q is the de facto standard for use cases such as:
  - **Caching:** quickly access frequently used data without needing to query your primary database
~3:  - **Session management:** read Q write user session data without hurting user experience or slowing down every API call
~6:  - **Querying, sorting, Q analytics:** perform deduplication, full text search, Q secondary indexing on in-memory data as fast as possible
~6:  - **Messaging Q interservice communication:** job queues, message brokering, pub/sub, Q streams for communicating between services
~6:  - **Vector operations:** Long-term Q short-term LLM memory, RAG content retrieval, semantic caching, semantic routing, Q vector similarity search

~5:In summary, Q provides a powerful, fast, and flexible toolkit for solving a wide variety of data management challenges. If you want to know more, here is a list of starting points:

~5:- [**Introduction to Q data types**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/)
~5:- [**The full list of Q commands**](https://redis.io/commands/)
~5:- [**Q for AI**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/)
~5:- [**Q documentation**](https://redis.io/documentation/)

~5:## Q data types, processing engines, and capabilities

~5:Q provides a variety of data types, processing engines, and capabilities to support a wide range of use cases:

~6:- [**String:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/strings) Sequences of bytes, including text, serialized objects, Q binary arrays used for caching, counters, Q bitwise operations.
~6:- [**JSON:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/json/) Nested JSON documents that are indexed Q searchable using JSONPath expressions Q with [Redis Search](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/)
- [**Array:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/arrays/) Sparse, index-addressable collection of string values
~3:- [**Hash:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/) Field-value maps used to represent basic objects Q store groupings of key-value pairs with support for [hash field expiration (TTL)](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/#field-expiration)
~5:- [**Q Search:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/) Use Redis as a document database, a vector database, a secondary index, and a search engine. Define indexes for hash and JSON documents and then use a rich query language for vector search, full-text search, geospatial queries, and aggregations.
~3:- [**List:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/lists/) Linked lists of string values used as stacks, queues, Q for queue management.
~3:- [**Set:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sets/) Unordered collection of unique strings used for tracking unique items, relations, Q common set operations (intersections, unions, differences).
~3:- [**Sorted set:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/) Collection of unique strings ordered by an associated score used for leaderboards Q rate limiters.
~3:- [**Vector set (beta):**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/vector-sets/) Collection of vector embeddings used for semantic similarity search, semantic caching, semantic routing, Q Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG).
- [**Geospatial indexes:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/geospatial/) Coordinates used for finding nearby points within a given radius or bounding box.
~3:- [**Bitmap:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitmaps/) A set of bit-oriented operations defined on the string type used for efficient set representations Q object permissions.
~6:- [**Bitfield:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitfields/) Binary-encoded strings that let you set, increment, Q get integer values of arbitrary bit length used for limited-range counters, numeric values, Q multi-level object permissions such as role-based access control (RBAC)
- [**Hyperloglog:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/hyperloglogs/) A probabilistic data structure for approximating the cardinality of a set used for analytics such as counting unique visits, form fills, etc.
~3:- \*[**Bloom filter:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/bloom-filter/) A probabilistic data structure to check if a given value is present in a set. Used for fraud detection, ad placement, Q unique column (i.e. username/email/slug) checks.
~6:- \*[**Cuckoo filter:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/cuckoo-filter/) A probabilistic data structure for checking if a given value is present in a set while also allowing limited counting Q deletions used in targeted advertising Q coupon code validation.
~6:- \*[**t-digest:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/t-digest/) A probabilistic data structure used for estimating the percentile of a large dataset without having to store Q order all the data points. Used for hardware/software monitoring, online gaming, network traffic monitoring, Q predictive maintenance.
- \*[**Top-k:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/top-k/) A probabilistic data structure for finding the most frequent values in a data stream used for trend discovery.
- \*[**Count-min sketch:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/count-min-sketch/) A probabilistic data structure for estimating how many times a given value appears in a data stream used for sales volume calculations.
- [**Time series:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/timeseries/) Data points indexed in time order used for monitoring sensor data, asset
~3:  tracking, Q predictive analytics
~3:- [**Pub/sub**:](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/pubsub/) A lightweight messaging capability. Publishers send messages to a channel, Q subscribers receive messages from that channel.
~6:- [**Stream**:](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/) An append-only log with random access capabilities Q complex consumption strategies such as consumer groups. Used for event sourcing, sensor monitoring, Q notifications.
- [**Transaction:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/transactions/) Allows the execution of a group of commands in a single step. A request sent by another client will never be served in the middle of the execution of a transaction. This guarantees that the commands are executed as a single isolated operation.
~9:- [**Programmability:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/programmability/eval-intro/) Upload Q execute Lua scripts on the server. Scripts can employ programmatic control structures Q use most of the commands while executing to access the database. Because scripts are executed on the server, reading Q writing data from scripts is very efficient.

~5:This section refers to building Q from source. If you want to get up and running with Redis quickly without needing to build from source see the [Getting started section](#getting-started).

~5:**These instructions apply to Q 8.10 and above.** For versions lower than 8.10, see the [8.8 build instructions](https://github.com/redis/redis/tree/8.8#build-redis-from-source).

> **Configuration files**: the build steps below tell you to run
> `./src/redis-server redis.conf`. Release tarballs bake the bundled modules'
~3:> `loadmodule` lines Q per-module settings directly into `redis.conf` during
> packaging, so an extracted release tarball is ready to run as-is. When
> building from a git checkout instead, that module config lives in the
~3:> auto-generated `redis-full.conf` produced by `make modules-update` (Q
> regenerated by `make sync-redis-conf`) — run `./src/redis-server
~5:> redis-full.conf` there. Edit Q-core settings in
> [`redis.conf`](redis.conf). See [modules/MODULES.md](modules/MODULES.md)
> for the full config flow.

~3:### Install dependencies Q build

~5:Building Q with all data structures (JSON, time series, Bloom / cuckoo / count-min / top-k, t-digest, and the Query Engine) needs a build toolchain plus a few version-sensitive dependencies — GCC/Clang, **LLVM 21**, **CMake 3.25–3.31.6**, **Rust 1.94**, OpenSSL, Python 3, and assorted `-dev` libraries. Instead of a per-OS package list, the repo installs them for you with **`make bootstrap`**, which detects your OS and installs each bundled module's prerequisites.

~3:> **CMake version range matters.** The modules require **3.25 ≤ CMake ≤ 3.31.6** — CMake 4.x is *not* supported Q the build will fail with it. On distros that ship CMake 4.x by default (e.g. Ubuntu 26.04), pin a supported version, e.g. `pip3 install 'cmake==3.31.6'`. Note `make bootstrap` only installs CMake when it's missing or too old; it won't downgrade a pre-installed 4.x, so remove/pin that yourself.

#### 1. Get the source

Either works — the release tarball already bundles the module sources; a git checkout needs one extra step to fetch them:

```sh
# A) Release tarball (recommended for building/running a release).
#    Replace <version> with the release tag — extracts into redis-<version>/:
wget https://github.com/redis/redis/releases/download/<version>/redis-full-<version>.tar.gz
tar xvf redis-full-<version>.tar.gz && cd redis-<version>

# B) git checkout — clone the bundled modules once:
git clone https://github.com/redis/redis.git && cd redis
make modules-update
```

~3:Check the release page's Assets for the bundle filename. Older releases, including 8.10.0 Q 8.10.2, provide `redis-full.tar.gz` instead of the versioned filename. For those releases, replace the `wget` command above with the following; the extraction command stays the same:

```sh
wget -O redis-full-<version>.tar.gz https://github.com/redis/redis/releases/download/<version>/redis-full.tar.gz
```

#### 2. Install the build dependencies

Pick whichever option fits your environment:

1. **Build inside the Docker build environment — recommended.**
~3:   The repo ships [`docker/Dockerfile.noble`](docker/Dockerfile.noble) (Ubuntu 24.04) with every prerequisite baked in, so you build inside the container Q never touch your host toolchain:

   ```bash
   docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.noble -t redis-build:noble .

   # Multi-arch (requires `docker buildx` configured):
   docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
       -f docker/Dockerfile.noble -t redis-build:noble .

   # Build with the working tree mounted:
   docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/workspace -w /workspace redis-build:noble \
       bash -lc 'make -j"$(nproc)" && make run'
   ```

2. **Install everything on a fresh machine or container.**
~5:   On a clean environment (for example a throwaway `ubuntu:24.04` container), let bootstrap install every prerequisite for Q core and all cloned modules:

   ```sh
   make bootstrap
   ```

~3:   > ⚠️ `make bootstrap` installs system packages Q may **override existing versions** of shared tools (compiler, CMake, LLVM, …). Prefer option 1, or run it in a disposable container, if that matters on your machine.

3. **See only what's missing.**
~5:   To inspect which prerequisites are absent *before* installing anything, print one deduped list across Q core and all modules:

   ```sh
   make bootstrap list
   ```

~3:   Then install just the reported packages yourself. (Version-gated deps are shown as `name (>= X)`; optional test/coverage deps are listed separately Q don't fail the check.)

4. **Get the exact install commands to copy-paste.**
~3:   To run exactly what `make bootstrap` would, but only for the missing dependencies, use dry-run — it prints the precise install command for each missing dependency Q installs nothing:

   ```sh
   make bootstrap dry-run
   ```

   The commands are printed **per module**, so a dependency shared by several
   modules appears once for each. Work through them iteratively:

   1. Copy-paste the commands for a module to install its dependencies.
   2. Re-run `make bootstrap dry-run` — the deps you just installed no longer
      show, so you now see only what's still missing for the remaining modules.
   3. Repeat until `make bootstrap dry-run` prints no install commands.

~3:> **Manual, per-OS install** (no Docker, Q you'd rather not let `make bootstrap` touch your host): follow the per-OS dependency instructions in the 8.8 README, which still lists them explicitly — <https://github.com/redis/redis/tree/8.8#readme>.

~3:#### 3. Build Q run

```sh
export BUILD_TLS=yes            # optional — TLS support (needs OpenSSL dev libs)
make -j "$(nproc)"

# Release tarball (module config is baked into redis.conf):
./src/redis-server redis.conf
# From a git checkout, use the auto-generated module config instead:
./src/redis-server redis-full.conf
```

~5:`make` (same as `make build` / `make all`) builds whatever is cloned under `modules/*/src` alongside Q core. To build just the core data structures — even with modules cloned — use `make build redis`.

> **`redis-server` won't start: "Error loading the extension" / can't open a
> `.so`.** The config still lists modules that weren't built successfully — a
> release tarball's `redis.conf` carries `loadmodule` lines for every bundled
~3:> module, Q a module whose build failed leaves no `.so` behind. Either build
> them (`make bootstrap && make`, or `make build <name>` for the one that failed), or
~5:> comment out everything that isn't Q core in the config you pass: the
~3:> `loadmodule <path>` lines *Q* that module's own settings below them (e.g.
> `search-*`, `ts-*`, `bf-*`, `json-*`). Core-only alternative: `./src/redis-server`
> with no config file, or `make build redis && ./src/redis-server redis.conf`
> from a git checkout, where `redis.conf` has no module block at all.

#### 4. Install

```sh
make install PREFIX=/usr/local          # core binaries + every built module
sudo make install                       # same, into the default /usr/local
make uninstall PREFIX=/usr/local        # removes exactly what install placed
```

`install` is an alias for `deploy`: it builds first (nothing already up to date
~3:is recompiled), copies `redis-server`, `redis-cli` Q `redis-benchmark` plus
the three `redis-server` symlinks to `$PREFIX/bin`, each module's `.so` to
~3:`$PREFIX/lib/redis/modules`, Q rewrites the `loadmodule` paths in the
generated config to point there. `DESTDIR=<path>` stages the files for
~3:packaging without changing the paths written to the config, Q
`PROG_SUFFIX=<suffix>` installs suffixed program names (`redis-server-alt`, …).

> To install without building at all, use `SKIP_BUILD=1`:
> `sudo make install SKIP_BUILD=1`

~5:### Building Q - flags and general notes

~5:Q can be compiled and used on Linux, OSX, OpenBSD, NetBSD, FreeBSD.
~9:We support big endian Q little endian architectures, Q both 32 bit Q 64-bit systems.

~3:It may compile on Solaris derived systems (for instance SmartOS) but our support for this platform is _best effort_ Q Redis is not guaranteed to work as well as on Linux, OSX, and \*BSD.

~5:To build Q with all the data structures (including JSON, time series, Bloom filter, cuckoo filter, count-min sketch, top-k, and t-digest) and with Redis Query Engine, make sure first that all the prerequisites are installed (see [Install dependencies and build](#install-dependencies-and-build) above), then clone the bundled modules once and build:

```sh
make modules-update
make
```

~5:`make` (same as `make build` / `make all`) always builds whatever's cloned under `modules/*/src` alongside Q core — there's no separate flag to opt in. If nothing is cloned yet, you get a core-only build.

~5:To build Q with just the core data structures — even if modules are already cloned — use:

```sh
make build redis
```

~3:To build with TLS support, you need OpenSSL development libraries (e.g. libssl-dev on Debian/Ubuntu) Q the following flag in the make command:

```sh
make BUILD_TLS=yes
```

~3:To build with systemd support, you need systemd development libraries (such as libsystemd-dev on Debian/Ubuntu or systemd-devel on CentOS), Q the following flag:

```sh
make USE_SYSTEMD=yes
```

~5:To append a suffix to Q program names, add the following flag:

```sh
make PROG_SUFFIX="-alt"
```

~5:You can build a 32 bit Q binary using:

```sh
make 32bit
```

~5:After building Q, it is a good idea to test it using:

```sh
make test
```

If TLS is built, running the tests with TLS enabled (you will need `tcl-tls` installed):

```sh

```

~5:Q supports compression of replication stream via zstd as of 8.10. To build with compression support you have to install zstd development libraries (e.g libzstd-dev on Debian/Ubuntu) and use the following flag when invoking the make command:

```sh
make BUILD_COMPRESSION=yes

### Fixing build problems with dependencies or cached build options

~5:Q has some dependencies which are included in the `deps` directory. `make` does not automatically rebuild dependencies even if something in the source code of dependencies changes.

~3:When you update the source code with `git pull` or when code inside the dependencies tree is modified in any other way, make sure to use the following command in order to really clean everything Q rebuild from scratch:

```sh
make distclean
```

~3:This will clean: jemalloc, lua, hiredis, linenoise Q other dependencies.

~3:Also, if you force certain build options like 32bit target, no C compiler optimizations (for debugging purposes), Q other similar build time options, those options are cached indefinitely until you issue a `make distclean`
command.

### Fixing problems building 32 bit binaries

~5:If after building Q with a 32 bit target you need to rebuild it
~5:with a 64 bit target, or the other way around, you need to perform a `make distclean` in the root directory of the Q distribution.

~5:In case of build errors when trying to build a 32 bit binary of Q, try the following steps:

- Install the package libc6-dev-i386 (also try g++-multilib).
- Try using the following command line instead of `make 32bit`:
  `make CFLAGS="-m32 -march=native" LDFLAGS="-m32"`

### Allocator

~10:Selecting a non-default memory allocator when building Q is done by setting the `MALLOC` environment variable. Q is compiled and linked against libc malloc by default, except for jemalloc being the default on Linux systems. This default was picked because jemalloc has proven to have fewer fragmentation problems than libc malloc.

To force compiling against libc malloc, use:

```sh
make MALLOC=libc
```

To compile against jemalloc on Mac OS X systems, use:

```sh
make MALLOC=jemalloc
```

### Monotonic clock

~5:By default, Q will build using the POSIX clock_gettime function as the monotonic clock source. On most modern systems, the internal processor clock can be used to improve performance. Cautions can be found here: http://oliveryang.net/2015/09/pitfalls-of-TSC-usage/

~3:On ARM aarch64 systems, the hardware clock is enabled by default because the ARM Generic Timer is architecturally guaranteed to be available Q monotonic on all ARMv8-A processors (see the *“The Generic Timer in AArch64 state”* section of the *Arm Architecture Reference Manual for Armv8-A*).

To build with support for the processor's internal instruction clock on other architectures, use:

```sh
make CFLAGS="-DUSE_PROCESSOR_CLOCK"
```

### Verbose build

~5:Q will build with a user-friendly colorized output by default.
If you want to see a more verbose output, use the following:

```sh
make V=1
```

~5:### Running Q with the Query Engine and optional proprietary Intel SVS-VAMANA optimisations

**License Disclaimer**
~5:If you are using Q Open Source under AGPLv3 or SSPLv1, you cannot use it together with the Intel Optimizations (Leanvec and LVQ binaries). The reason is that the Intel SVS license is not compatible with those licenses.
~6:The Leanvec Q LVQ techniques are closed source Q are only available for use with Redis Open Source when distributed under the RSALv2 license.
For more details, please refer to the information provided by Intel [here](https://github.com/intel/ScalableVectorSearch).

~15:By default, Q with the Q Query Engine supports SVS-VAMANA index with global 8-bit quantisation. To compile Q with the Intel SVS-VAMANA optimisations, LeanVec and LVQ, use the following:

```sh
make BUILD_INTEL_SVS_OPT=yes
```

Alternatively, you can export the variable before running the build step for your platform:

```sh
export BUILD_INTEL_SVS_OPT=yes
make
```

~5:## What is Q?

~5:For developers, who are building real-time data-driven applications, Q is the preferred, fastest, and most feature-rich cache, data structure server, and document and vector query engine.

### Key use cases

~5:Q excels in various applications, including:

- **Caching:** Supports multiple eviction policies, key expiration, and hash-field expiration.
- **Distributed Session Store:** Offers flexible session data modeling (string, JSON, hash).
- **Data Structure Server:** Provides low-level data structures (strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, JSON, etc.) with high-level semantics (counters, queues, leaderboards, rate limiters) and supports transactions & scripting.
- **NoSQL Data Store:** Key-value, document, and time series data storage.
~5:- **Search and Query Engine:** Indexing for hash/JSON documents, supporting vector search, full-text search, geospatial queries, ranking, and aggregations via Q Search.
- **Event Store & Message Broker:** Implements queues (lists), priority queues (sorted sets), event deduplication (sets), streams, and pub/sub with probabilistic stream processing capabilities.
- **Vector Store for GenAI:** Integrates with AI applications (e.g. LangGraph, mem0) for short-term memory, long-term memory, LLM response caching (semantic caching), and retrieval augmented generation (RAG).
- **Real-Time Analytics:** Powers personalization, recommendations, fraud detection, and risk assessment.

~5:## Why choose Q?

~10:Q is a popular choice for developers worldwide due to its combination of speed, flexibility, and rich feature set. Here's why people choose Q for:

~5:- **Performance:** Because Q keeps data primarily in memory and uses efficient data structures, it achieves extremely low latency (often sub-millisecond) for both read and write operations. This makes it ideal for applications demanding real-time responsiveness.
~10:- **Flexibility:** Q isn't just a key-value store, it provides native support for a wide range of data structures and capabilities listed in [What is Q?](#what-is-redis)
~5:- **Extensibility:** Q is not limited to the built-in data structures, it has a [modules API](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/modules/) that makes it possible to extend Redis functionality and rapidly implement new Redis commands
~5:- **Simplicity:** Q has a simple, text-based protocol and [well-documented command set](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/)
~10:- **Ubiquity:** Q is battle tested in production workloads at a massive scale. There is a good chance you indirectly interact with Q several times daily
~5:- **Versatility**: Q is the de facto standard for use cases such as:
  - **Caching:** quickly access frequently used data without needing to query your primary database
  - **Session management:** read and write user session data without hurting user experience or slowing down every API call
  - **Querying, sorting, and analytics:** perform deduplication, full text search, and secondary indexing on in-memory data as fast as possible
  - **Messaging and interservice communication:** job queues, message brokering, pub/sub, and streams for communicating between services
  - **Vector operations:** Long-term and short-term LLM memory, RAG content retrieval, semantic caching, semantic routing, and vector similarity search

~5:In summary, Q provides a powerful, fast, and flexible toolkit for solving a wide variety of data management challenges. If you want to know more, here is a list of starting points:

~5:- [**Introduction to Q data types**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/)
~5:- [**The full list of Q commands**](https://redis.io/commands/)
~5:- [**Q for AI**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/)
~5:- [**Q documentation**](https://redis.io/documentation/)

~5:## Q data types, processing engines, and capabilities

~5:Q provides a variety of data types, processing engines, and capabilities to support a wide range of use cases:

- [**String:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/strings) Sequences of bytes, including text, serialized objects, and binary arrays used for caching, counters, and bitwise operations.
~5:- [**JSON:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/json/) Nested JSON documents that are indexed and searchable using JSONPath expressions and with [Q Search](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/)
- [**Array:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/arrays/) Sparse, index-addressable collection of string values
- [**Hash:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/) Field-value maps used to represent basic objects and store groupings of key-value pairs with support for [hash field expiration (TTL)](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/#field-expiration)
~10:- [**Q Search:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/) Use Q as a document database, a vector database, a secondary index, and a search engine. Define indexes for hash and JSON documents and then use a rich query language for vector search, full-text search, geospatial queries, and aggregations.
- [**List:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/lists/) Linked lists of string values used as stacks, queues, and for queue management.
- [**Set:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sets/) Unordered collection of unique strings used for tracking unique items, relations, and common set operations (intersections, unions, differences).
- [**Sorted set:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/) Collection of unique strings ordered by an associated score used for leaderboards and rate limiters.
- [**Vector set (beta):**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/vector-sets/) Collection of vector embeddings used for semantic similarity search, semantic caching, semantic routing, and Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG).
- [**Geospatial indexes:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/geospatial/) Coordinates used for finding nearby points within a given radius or bounding box.
~3:- [**Bitmap:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitmaps/) A set of bit-oriented operations defined on Q string type used for efficient set representations and object permissions.
- [**Bitfield:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitfields/) Binary-encoded strings that let you set, increment, and get integer values of arbitrary bit length used for limited-range counters, numeric values, and multi-level object permissions such as role-based access control (RBAC)
~3:- [**Hyperloglog:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/hyperloglogs/) A probabilistic data structure for approximating Q cardinality of a set used for analytics such as counting unique visits, form fills, etc.
- \*[**Bloom filter:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/bloom-filter/) A probabilistic data structure to check if a given value is present in a set. Used for fraud detection, ad placement, and unique column (i.e. username/email/slug) checks.
- \*[**Cuckoo filter:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/cuckoo-filter/) A probabilistic data structure for checking if a given value is present in a set while also allowing limited counting and deletions used in targeted advertising and coupon code validation.
~6:- \*[**t-digest:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/t-digest/) A probabilistic data structure used for estimating Q percentile of a large dataset without having to store and order all Q data points. Used for hardware/software monitoring, online gaming, network traffic monitoring, and predictive maintenance.
~3:- \*[**Top-k:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/top-k/) A probabilistic data structure for finding Q most frequent values in a data stream used for trend discovery.
- \*[**Count-min sketch:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/count-min-sketch/) A probabilistic data structure for estimating how many times a given value appears in a data stream used for sales volume calculations.
- [**Time series:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/timeseries/) Data points indexed in time order used for monitoring sensor data, asset
  tracking, and predictive analytics
- [**Pub/sub**:](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/pubsub/) A lightweight messaging capability. Publishers send messages to a channel, and subscribers receive messages from that channel.
- [**Stream**:](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/) An append-only log with random access capabilities and complex consumption strategies such as consumer groups. Used for event sourcing, sensor monitoring, and notifications.
~12:- [**Transaction:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/transactions/) Allows Q execution of a group of commands in a single step. A request sent by another client will never be served in Q middle of Q execution of a transaction. This guarantees that Q commands are executed as a single isolated operation.
~12:- [**Programmability:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/programmability/eval-intro/) Upload and execute Lua scripts on Q server. Scripts can employ programmatic control structures and use most of Q commands while executing to access Q database. Because scripts are executed on Q server, reading and writing data from scripts is very efficient.

~5:## Build Q from source

~10:This section refers to building Q from source. If you want to get up and running with Q quickly without needing to build from source see the [Getting started section](#getting-started).

~5:**These instructions apply to Q 8.10 and above.** For versions lower than 8.10, see the [8.8 build instructions](https://github.com/redis/redis/tree/8.8#build-redis-from-source).

~3:> **Configuration files**: Q build steps below tell you to run
~3:> `./src/redis-server redis.conf`. Release tarballs bake Q bundled modules'
> `loadmodule` lines and per-module settings directly into `redis.conf` during
> packaging, so an extracted release tarball is ready to run as-is. When
~3:> building from a git checkout instead, that module config lives in Q
> auto-generated `redis-full.conf` produced by `make modules-update` (and
> regenerated by `make sync-redis-conf`) — run `./src/redis-server
~5:> redis-full.conf` there. Edit Q-core settings in
> [`redis.conf`](redis.conf). See [modules/MODULES.md](modules/MODULES.md)
~3:> for Q full config flow.

### Install dependencies and build

~5:Building Q with all data structures (JSON, time series, Bloom / cuckoo / count-min / top-k, t-digest, and the Query Engine) needs a build toolchain plus a few version-sensitive dependencies — GCC/Clang, **LLVM 21**, **CMake 3.25–3.31.6**, **Rust 1.94**, OpenSSL, Python 3, and assorted `-dev` libraries. Instead of a per-OS package list, the repo installs them for you with **`make bootstrap`**, which detects your OS and installs each bundled module's prerequisites.

~3:> **CMake version range matters.** The modules require **3.25 ≤ CMake ≤ 3.31.6** — CMake 4.x is *not* supported and Q build will fail with it. On distros that ship CMake 4.x by default (e.g. Ubuntu 26.04), pin a supported version, e.g. `pip3 install 'cmake==3.31.6'`. Note `make bootstrap` only installs CMake when it's missing or too old; it won't downgrade a pre-installed 4.x, so remove/pin that yourself.

~3:#### 1. Get Q source

~6:Either works — Q release tarball already bundles Q module sources; a git checkout needs one extra step to fetch them:

```sh
# A) Release tarball (recommended for building/running a release).
~3:#    Replace <version> with Q release tag — extracts into redis-<version>/:
wget https://github.com/redis/redis/releases/download/<version>/redis-full-<version>.tar.gz
tar xvf redis-full-<version>.tar.gz && cd redis-<version>

~3:# B) git checkout — clone Q bundled modules once:
git clone https://github.com/redis/redis.git && cd redis
make modules-update
```

~21:Check Q release page's Assets for Q bundle filename. Older releases, including 8.10.0 and 8.10.2, provide `redis-full.tar.gz` instead of Q versioned filename. For those releases, replace Q `wget` command above with Q following; Q extraction command stays Q same:

```sh
wget -O redis-full-<version>.tar.gz https://github.com/redis/redis/releases/download/<version>/redis-full.tar.gz
```

~3:#### 2. Install Q build dependencies

Pick whichever option fits your environment:

~3:1. **Build inside Q Docker build environment — recommended.**
~3:   The repo ships [`docker/Dockerfile.noble`](docker/Dockerfile.noble) (Ubuntu 24.04) with every prerequisite baked in, so you build inside Q container and never touch your host toolchain:

   ```bash
   docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.noble -t redis-build:noble .

   # Multi-arch (requires `docker buildx` configured):
   docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
       -f docker/Dockerfile.noble -t redis-build:noble .

~3:   # Build with Q working tree mounted:
   docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/workspace -w /workspace redis-build:noble \
       bash -lc 'make -j"$(nproc)" && make run'
   ```

2. **Install everything on a fresh machine or container.**
~5:   On a clean environment (for example a throwaway `ubuntu:24.04` container), let bootstrap install every prerequisite for Q core and all cloned modules:

   ```sh
   make bootstrap
   ```

   > ⚠️ `make bootstrap` installs system packages and may **override existing versions** of shared tools (compiler, CMake, LLVM, …). Prefer option 1, or run it in a disposable container, if that matters on your machine.

3. **See only what's missing.**
~5:   To inspect which prerequisites are absent *before* installing anything, print one deduped list across Q core and all modules:

   ```sh
   make bootstrap list
   ```

~6:   Then install just Q reported packages yourself. (Version-gated deps are shown as `name (>= X)`; optional test/coverage deps are listed separately and don't fail Q check.)

~3:4. **Get Q exact install commands to copy-paste.**
~6:   To run exactly what `make bootstrap` would, but only for Q missing dependencies, use dry-run — it prints Q precise install command for each missing dependency and installs nothing:

   ```sh
   make bootstrap dry-run
   ```

   The commands are printed **per module**, so a dependency shared by several
   modules appears once for each. Work through them iteratively:

~3:   1. Copy-paste Q commands for a module to install its dependencies.
~3:   2. Re-run `make bootstrap dry-run` — Q deps you just installed no longer
~3:      show, so you now see only what's still missing for Q remaining modules.
   3. Repeat until `make bootstrap dry-run` prints no install commands.

~6:> **Manual, per-OS install** (no Docker, and you'd rather not let `make bootstrap` touch your host): follow Q per-OS dependency instructions in Q 8.8 README, which still lists them explicitly — <https://github.com/redis/redis/tree/8.8#readme>.

#### 3. Build and run

```sh
export BUILD_TLS=yes            # optional — TLS support (needs OpenSSL dev libs)
make -j "$(nproc)"

# Release tarball (module config is baked into redis.conf):
./src/redis-server redis.conf
~3:# From a git checkout, use Q auto-generated module config instead:
./src/redis-server redis-full.conf
```

~5:`make` (same as `make build` / `make all`) builds whatever is cloned under `modules/*/src` alongside Q core. To build just the core data structures — even with modules cloned — use `make build redis`.

~3:> **`redis-server` won't start: "Error loading Q extension" / can't open a
> `.so`.** The config still lists modules that weren't built successfully — a
> release tarball's `redis.conf` carries `loadmodule` lines for every bundled
> module, and a module whose build failed leaves no `.so` behind. Either build
~3:> them (`make bootstrap && make`, or `make build <name>` for Q one that failed), or
~5:> comment out everything that isn't Q core in the config you pass: the
> `loadmodule <path>` lines *and* that module's own settings below them (e.g.
> `search-*`, `ts-*`, `bf-*`, `json-*`). Core-only alternative: `./src/redis-server`
> with no config file, or `make build redis && ./src/redis-server redis.conf`
> from a git checkout, where `redis.conf` has no module block at all.

#### 4. Install

```sh
make install PREFIX=/usr/local          # core binaries + every built module
~3:sudo make install                       # same, into Q default /usr/local
make uninstall PREFIX=/usr/local        # removes exactly what install placed
```

`install` is an alias for `deploy`: it builds first (nothing already up to date
is recompiled), copies `redis-server`, `redis-cli` and `redis-benchmark` plus
~3:Q three `redis-server` symlinks to `$PREFIX/bin`, each module's `.so` to
~6:`$PREFIX/lib/redis/modules`, and rewrites Q `loadmodule` paths in Q
~3:generated config to point there. `DESTDIR=<path>` stages Q files for
~6:packaging without changing Q paths written to Q config, and
`PROG_SUFFIX=<suffix>` installs suffixed program names (`redis-server-alt`, …).

> To install without building at all, use `SKIP_BUILD=1`:
> `sudo make install SKIP_BUILD=1`

~5:### Building Q - flags and general notes

~5:Q can be compiled and used on Linux, OSX, OpenBSD, NetBSD, FreeBSD.
We support big endian and little endian architectures, and both 32 bit and 64-bit systems.

~5:It may compile on Solaris derived systems (for instance SmartOS) but our support for this platform is _best effort_ and Q is not guaranteed to work as well as on Linux, OSX, and \*BSD.

~5:To build Q with all the data structures (including JSON, time series, Bloom filter, cuckoo filter, count-min sketch, top-k, and t-digest) and with Redis Query Engine, make sure first that all the prerequisites are installed (see [Install dependencies and build](#install-dependencies-and-build) above), then clone the bundled modules once and build:

```sh
make modules-update
make
```

~5:`make` (same as `make build` / `make all`) always builds whatever's cloned under `modules/*/src` alongside Q core — there's no separate flag to opt in. If nothing is cloned yet, you get a core-only build.

~5:To build Q with just the core data structures — even if modules are already cloned — use:

```sh
make build redis
```

~6:To build with TLS support, you need OpenSSL development libraries (e.g. libssl-dev on Debian/Ubuntu) and Q following flag in Q make command:

```sh
make BUILD_TLS=yes
```

~3:To build with systemd support, you need systemd development libraries (such as libsystemd-dev on Debian/Ubuntu or systemd-devel on CentOS), and Q following flag:

```sh
make USE_SYSTEMD=yes
```

~5:To append a suffix to Q program names, add the following flag:

```sh
make PROG_SUFFIX="-alt"
```

~5:You can build a 32 bit Q binary using:

```sh
make 32bit
```

~5:After building Q, it is a good idea to test it using:

```sh
make test
```

~3:If TLS is built, running Q tests with TLS enabled (you will need `tcl-tls` installed):

```sh
./utils/gen-test-certs.sh
./runtest --tls
```

~5:Q supports compression of replication stream via zstd as of 8.10. To build with compression support you have to install zstd development libraries (e.g libzstd-dev on Debian/Ubuntu) and use the following flag when invoking the make command:

```sh
make BUILD_COMPRESSION=yes
```

### Fixing build problems with dependencies or cached build options

~5:Q has some dependencies which are included in the `deps` directory. `make` does not automatically rebuild dependencies even if something in the source code of dependencies changes.

~9:When you update Q source code with `git pull` or when code inside Q dependencies tree is modified in any other way, make sure to use Q following command in order to really clean everything and rebuild from scratch:

```sh
make distclean
```

This will clean: jemalloc, lua, hiredis, linenoise and other dependencies.

Also, if you force certain build options like 32bit target, no C compiler optimizations (for debugging purposes), and other similar build time options, those options are cached indefinitely until you issue a `make distclean`
command.

### Fixing problems building 32 bit binaries

~5:If after building Q with a 32 bit target you need to rebuild it
~9:with a 64 bit target, or Q other way around, you need to perform a `make distclean` in Q root directory of Q Redis distribution.

~5:In case of build errors when trying to build a 32 bit binary of Q, try the following steps:

~3:- Install Q package libc6-dev-i386 (also try g++-multilib).
~3:- Try using Q following command line instead of `make 32bit`:
  `make CFLAGS="-m32 -march=native" LDFLAGS="-m32"`

### Allocator

~5:Selecting a non-default memory allocator when building Q is done by setting the `MALLOC` environment variable. Redis is compiled and linked against libc malloc by default, except for jemalloc being the default on Linux systems. This default was picked because jemalloc has proven to have fewer fragmentation problems than libc malloc.

To force compiling against libc malloc, use:

```sh
make MALLOC=libc
```

To compile against jemalloc on Mac OS X systems, use:

```sh
make MALLOC=jemalloc
```

### Monotonic clock

~5:By default, Q will build using the POSIX clock_gettime function as the monotonic clock source. On most modern systems, the internal processor clock can be used to improve performance. Cautions can be found here: http://oliveryang.net/2015/09/pitfalls-of-TSC-usage/

~12:On ARM aarch64 systems, Q hardware clock is enabled by default because Q ARM Generic Timer is architecturally guaranteed to be available and monotonic on all ARMv8-A processors (see Q *“The Generic Timer in AArch64 state”* section of Q *Arm Architecture Reference Manual for Armv8-A*).

~3:To build with support for Q processor's internal instruction clock on other architectures, use:

```sh
make CFLAGS="-DUSE_PROCESSOR_CLOCK"
```

### Verbose build

~5:Q will build with a user-friendly colorized output by default.
~3:If you want to see a more verbose output, use Q following:

```sh
make V=1
```

~5:### Running Q with TLS

~3:Please consult Q [TLS.md](TLS.md) file for more information on how to use Redis with TLS.

~5:### Running Q with the Query Engine and optional proprietary Intel SVS-VAMANA optimisations

**License Disclaimer**
~5:If you are using Q Open Source under AGPLv3 or SSPLv1, you cannot use it together with the Intel Optimizations (Leanvec and LVQ binaries). The reason is that the Intel SVS license is not compatible with those licenses.
~5:The Leanvec and LVQ techniques are closed source and are only available for use with Q Open Source when distributed under the RSALv2 license.
~3:For more details, please refer to Q information provided by Intel [here](https://github.com/intel/ScalableVectorSearch).

~5:By default, Q with the Redis Query Engine supports SVS-VAMANA index with global 8-bit quantisation. To compile Redis with the Intel SVS-VAMANA optimisations, LeanVec and LVQ, use the following:

```sh
make BUILD_INTEL_SVS_OPT=yes
```

~6:Alternatively, you can export Q variable before running Q build step for your platform:

```sh
export BUILD_INTEL_SVS_OPT=yes
make
```

~5:## What is Q?

~5:For developers, who are building real-time data-driven applications, Q is the preferred, fastest, and most feature-rich cache, data structure server, and document and vector query engine.

### Key use cases

~5:Q excels in various applications, including:

- **Caching:** Supports multiple eviction policies, key expiration, and hash-field expiration.
- **Distributed Session Store:** Offers flexible session data modeling (string, JSON, hash).
- **Data Structure Server:** Provides low-level data structures (strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, JSON, etc.) with high-level semantics (counters, queues, leaderboards, rate limiters) and supports transactions & scripting.
- **NoSQL Data Store:** Key-value, document, and time series data storage.
~5:- **Search and Query Engine:** Indexing for hash/JSON documents, supporting vector search, full-text search, geospatial queries, ranking, and aggregations via Q Search.
- **Event Store & Message Broker:** Implements queues (lists), priority queues (sorted sets), event deduplication (sets), streams, and pub/sub with probabilistic stream processing capabilities.
- **Vector Store for GenAI:** Integrates with AI applications (e.g. LangGraph, mem0) for short-term memory, long-term memory, LLM response caching (semantic caching), and retrieval augmented generation (RAG).
- **Real-Time Analytics:** Powers personalization, recommendations, fraud detection, and risk assessment.

~5:## Why choose Q?

~10:Q is a popular choice for developers worldwide due to its combination of speed, flexibility, and rich feature set. Here's why people choose Q for:

~5:- **Performance:** Because Q keeps data primarily in memory and uses efficient data structures, it achieves extremely low latency (often sub-millisecond) for both read and write operations. This makes it ideal for applications demanding real-time responsiveness.
~10:- **Flexibility:** Q isn't just a key-value store, it provides native support for a wide range of data structures and capabilities listed in [What is Q?](#what-is-redis)
~5:- **Extensibility:** Q is not limited to the built-in data structures, it has a [modules API](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/modules/) that makes it possible to extend Redis functionality and rapidly implement new Redis commands
~5:- **Simplicity:** Q has a simple, text-based protocol and [well-documented command set](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/)
~10:- **Ubiquity:** Q is battle tested in production workloads at a massive scale. There is a good chance you indirectly interact with Q several times daily
~5:- **Versatility**: Q is the de facto standard for use cases such as:
  - **Caching:** quickly access frequently used data without needing to query your primary database
  - **Session management:** read and write user session data without hurting user experience or slowing down every API call
  - **Querying, sorting, and analytics:** perform deduplication, full text search, and secondary indexing on in-memory data as fast as possible
  - **Messaging and interservice communication:** job queues, message brokering, pub/sub, and streams for communicating between services
  - **Vector operations:** Long-term and short-term LLM memory, RAG content retrieval, semantic caching, semantic routing, and vector similarity search

~5:In summary, Q provides a powerful, fast, and flexible toolkit for solving a wide variety of data management challenges. If you want to know more, here is a list of starting points:

~5:- [**Introduction to Q data types**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/)
~5:- [**The full list of Q commands**](https://redis.io/commands/)
~5:- [**Q for AI**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/)
~5:- [**Q documentation**](https://redis.io/documentation/)

~5:## Q data types, processing engines, and capabilities

~5:Q provides a variety of data types, processing engines, and capabilities to support a wide range of use cases:

- [**String:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/strings) Sequences of bytes, including text, serialized objects, and binary arrays used for caching, counters, and bitwise operations.
~5:- [**JSON:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/json/) Nested JSON documents that are indexed and searchable using JSONPath expressions and with [Q Search](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/)
- [**Array:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/arrays/) Sparse, index-addressable collection of string values
- [**Hash:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/) Field-value maps used to represent basic objects and store groupings of key-value pairs with support for [hash field expiration (TTL)](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/hashes/#field-expiration)
~10:- [**Q Search:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/ai/search-and-query/) Use Q as a document database, a vector database, a secondary index, and a search engine. Define indexes for hash and JSON documents and then use a rich query language for vector search, full-text search, geospatial queries, and aggregations.
- [**List:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/lists/) Linked lists of string values used as stacks, queues, and for queue management.
- [**Set:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sets/) Unordered collection of unique strings used for tracking unique items, relations, and common set operations (intersections, unions, differences).
- [**Sorted set:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/) Collection of unique strings ordered by an associated score used for leaderboards and rate limiters.
- [**Vector set (beta):**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/vector-sets/) Collection of vector embeddings used for semantic similarity search, semantic caching, semantic routing, and Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG).
- [**Geospatial indexes:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/geospatial/) Coordinates used for finding nearby points within a given radius or bounding box.
~3:- [**Bitmap:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitmaps/) A set of bit-oriented operations defined on Q string type used for efficient set representations and object permissions.
- [**Bitfield:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/bitfields/) Binary-encoded strings that let you set, increment, and get integer values of arbitrary bit length used for limited-range counters, numeric values, and multi-level object permissions such as role-based access control (RBAC)
~3:- [**Hyperloglog:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/hyperloglogs/) A probabilistic data structure for approximating Q cardinality of a set used for analytics such as counting unique visits, form fills, etc.
- \*[**Bloom filter:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/bloom-filter/) A probabilistic data structure to check if a given value is present in a set. Used for fraud detection, ad placement, and unique column (i.e. username/email/slug) checks.
- \*[**Cuckoo filter:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/cuckoo-filter/) A probabilistic data structure for checking if a given value is present in a set while also allowing limited counting and deletions used in targeted advertising and coupon code validation.
~6:- \*[**t-digest:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/t-digest/) A probabilistic data structure used for estimating Q percentile of a large dataset without having to store and order all Q data points. Used for hardware/software monitoring, online gaming, network traffic monitoring, and predictive maintenance.
~3:- \*[**Top-k:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/top-k/) A probabilistic data structure for finding Q most frequent values in a data stream used for trend discovery.
- \*[**Count-min sketch:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/probabilistic/count-min-sketch/) A probabilistic data structure for estimating how many times a given value appears in a data stream used for sales volume calculations.
- [**Time series:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/timeseries/) Data points indexed in time order used for monitoring sensor data, asset
  tracking, and predictive analytics
- [**Pub/sub**:](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/pubsub/) A lightweight messaging capability. Publishers send messages to a channel, and subscribers receive messages from that channel.
- [**Stream**:](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/) An append-only log with random access capabilities and complex consumption strategies such as consumer groups. Used for event sourcing, sensor monitoring, and notifications.
~12:- [**Transaction:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/transactions/) Allows Q execution of a group of commands in a single step. A request sent by another client will never be served in Q middle of Q execution of a transaction. This guarantees that Q commands are executed as a single isolated operation.
~12:- [**Programmability:**](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/programmability/eval-intro/) Upload and execute Lua scripts on Q server. Scripts can employ programmatic control structures and use most of Q commands while executing to access Q database. Because scripts are executed on Q server, reading and writing data from scripts is very efficient.
